extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, and journalists seeking an overview of ProPublica and its practices
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia article summarizing ProPublica's mission, history, funding, notable projects, partnerships, and editorial practices; useful for understanding how the organization produces and distributes investigative journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staff-led investigative reporting and partner distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigations are conducted by its staff of full-time reporters, and the resulting stories are distributed to news partners for publication or broadcast. In some cases, reporters from both ProPublica and its partners work together on a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model emphasizes dedicated in-house investigative reporters plus collaborative co-publication with external news organizations to expand reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative Commons licensing for published work
rubrics_metrics.description: The newsgroup shares its work under the Creative Commons no-derivative, non-commercial license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content reuse is permitted only under the specified Creative Commons terms (no derivatives, non-commercial); this is a firm licensing policy affecting distribution and republishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial independence from funders
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizational structure and board set-up intended so that the board does not know in advance what ProPublica will report on, to maintain independence and nonpartisanship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ProPublica's reported approach (per Paul Steiger) is to build governance that prevents funders or trustees from influencing reporting choices; practical implication: maintain firewalls and disclosure to preserve credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about funding and donor relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: The article lists ProPublica's funding sources (Sandler Foundation, Knight, MacArthur, Pew, Ford, Carnegie, Atlantic Philanthropies, and others) and notes links between foundation trustees and ProPublica leadership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public disclosure of major donors, grants, and any overlaps between donors and board/trustees is presented as a transparency practice and is relevant to assessing independence and potential conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local Reporting Network partnership and eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The Local Reporting Network consists of partnerships with local news organizations. The network subsidizes salary and benefits for reporters, who must apply together with a local news organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eligibility and selection are tied to joint applications (reporter + local newsroom) and selection decisions by the network; policy supports embedding funded reporters at local outlets to produce collaborative local investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowdsourced data collection and newsroom collaboration (Documenting Hate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Documenting Hate allows victims or witnesses of hate crime incidents to submit stories and allows journalists and newsrooms to partner with ProPublica to write stories based on the dataset they are collecting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Project design mixes public submissions (crowdsourcing) with data collection and external newsroom partnerships to enable reporting from aggregated incidents; highlights processes for sourcing and collaborating on data-driven civil-rights reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data-driven public-facing tools and explainable presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Projects like the cancer-causing industrial air pollution map and the Surgeon Scorecard convert large administrative datasets into interactive, neighborhood-level tools intended to represent data in a way the public can understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasis on building interactive databases and maps that translate complex datasets into accessible visuals and narratives; expectation to document methodology and make findings actionable (e.g., prompting agency monitoring).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological transparency and readiness to respond to critique
rubrics_metrics.description: The Surgeon Scorecard prompted methodological criticism from RAND and other commentators; ProPublica published rebuttals and defended the decision to make opaque medical data more visible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard practice implied: publish methodology, anticipate independent methodological critique, and provide specific rebuttals or corrections when appropriate to defend analytic choices and maintain credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections and retractions policy (public correction of errors)
rubrics_metrics.description: ProPublica published an investigative report about Gina Haspel in 2017 and in 2018 retracted part of that report when facts about timing of events were found to be incorrect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implied editorial standard: issue public corrections/retractions when reporting errors are identified; correction process is part of maintaining journalistic integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative investigative projects and co-publication crediting
rubrics_metrics.description: ProPublica has a history of collaborative projects (e.g., with The Marshall Project, New York Times Magazine, Los Angeles Times) where reporting teams from ProPublica and partner outlets work jointly and share bylines/credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collaboration model involves joint investigations, shared reporting responsibilities, and co-publication arrangements to amplify impact and combine resources/expertise.
